Below is a synthesis of why published outcomes for scapholunate ligament (SLL) reconstruction often conflict across techniques, followed by evidence-based explanations and practical implications.

Technique diversity and unresolved superiority
- Multiple operative strategies have been described for chronic scapholunate instability, spanning primary repair/capsulodesis, tendon graft tenodesis (e.g., 3‑ligament tenodesis), bone‑ligament‑bone or interposition “bone bridge” reconstructions, and newer suspension or anchor‑based methods; there is no consensus on a single best approach, and reported results vary across series and timepoints <cite id="94179f19-4">There are many arthroscopic techniques to treat chronic scapholunate injuries such as scapholunate ligament primary repair using various types of capsulodesis, tendon graft reconstruction, bone-ligament-bone procedure, various intercarpal fusions and proximal row carpectomy, total wrist fusion and arthroplasty; early diagnosis and management are necessary to preserve wrist function</cite> <cite id="2c329394-2">There is currently no consensus on the best operative treatment for chronic scapholunate dissociation without degenerative change; numerous procedures (dorsal capsulodesis, bone‑ligament‑bone autografts, SLAM, RASL, tendon reconstruction) have unsatisfactory results; 3‑ligament tenodesis is commonly used but can loosen and recur; the Mark‑Henry technique reconstructs both volar/dorsal limbs but has complications like fractures and lunate avascular necrosis</cite>. 
- Even within tenodesis, subtypes differ biomechanically and clinically (e.g., Corella, SLAM, modified Brunelli), with cadaveric/FEA work showing technique‑dependent restoration of SL gap and angle across wrist positions; this mechanical variability plausibly maps to variable radiographic and patient‑reported outcomes across cohorts <cite id="94179f19-3">The Corella technique restored SL gap/angle closer to intact ligament than SLAM and modified Brunelli across flexion/extension/radial‑ulnar deviation, with multiple junction points between scaphoid and lunate being beneficial</cite>. 
- Single‑series outcomes can be favorable for specific techniques (e.g., palmaris longus suture‑anchor reconstruction with DASH/Mayo scores comparable to tenodesis and high satisfaction), yet sample sizes and indications differ, contributing to cross‑study disparity <cite id="94179f19-2">A palmaris longus, suture‑anchor SL reconstruction series reported mid‑term outcomes comparable to tenodesis with high return to employment and satisfaction</cite>.

Biomechanical and fixation‑related reasons for conflicting outcomes
- Technique choice alters scapholunate kinematics and load sharing. Tenodesis methods that distribute load across multiple carpal ligaments may better resist multidirectional instability than single‑junction capsulodesis, but over‑constraint or malpositioning can cause complications (e.g., lunate necrosis, tunnel fractures) that worsen outcomes <cite id="2c329394-2">3‑LT has favorable but recurrent loosening and radiographic abnormalities; Mark‑Henry reconstructs both volar/dorsal limbs yet has complications including fractures and avascular necrosis of the lunate</cite> <cite id="94179f19-3">Corella outperformed SLAM and modified Brunelli in restoring gap/angle across wrist positions, supporting the value of multiple junction points</cite>. 
- Anchor‑based “suspension” strategies avoid drilling through bone for graft fixation and aim to harness high pullout strength, but outcomes depend on suture configuration, graft tensioning, and whether both palmar/dorsal spans are adequately fixed; small series suggest satisfactory results but broader experience shows variable radiographic healing and complications when compared across techniques <cite id="94179f19-2">Palmaris longus reconstruction with bone anchors achieved functional outcomes comparable to tenodesis and avoided drilling through bone</cite> <cite id="2c329394-1">A non–bone tunnel technique reported clinical outcomes, highlighting technique variation</cite>. 
- Palmar‑only approaches can be less invasive and preserve blood supply but risk incomplete stabilization if the stronger palmar SL ligament isn’t adequately sutured, with reported complications including limited ROM, avascular necrosis, or subchondral sclerosis in some cases—factors that explain divergent outcome narratives depending on fixation completeness <cite id="2c329394-3">Palmar approach may reduce stiffness and preserve vascularity; complications (limited ROM, avascular necrosis or sclerosis, scaphoid flexion deformity) have been described when dorsal fixation or palmar suture is inadequate</cite>.

Biological/tissue and timing factors that shift outcomes
- Chronicity and scaphoid integrity fundamentally change tissue quality and healing potential. In acute injuries, early repair/capsulodesis yields better ligamentous healing; in chronic cases with degenerative change or irreparable SLIL, reconstructions (autograft, bone bridge) are often required, but outcomes degrade with advanced arthritis, cartilage injury, or persistent instability despite reconstruction <cite id="2c329394-0">Acute repair remains the gold standard because earlier intervention provides better results; for chronic injuries, ligament reconstruction is generally preferable, with many arthroscopic options when immobilization fails</cite> <cite id="2c329394-2">When degenerative change is present, best technique remains uncertain; bone‑ligament‑bone autografts and tenodesis are selected, yet results are unsatisfactory and a single best method is undetermined</cite>. 
- Graft choice and tissue quality modulate healing. Biomechanical loosening of tenodesis over time and the need to reconstruct both volar/dorsal limbs (as in Mark‑Henry) reflect biological creep and multidirectional insufficiency; complications like avascular necrosis may arise from altered load transfer and soft‑tissue handling, especially if palmar stabilizers are not robustly reconstructed <cite id="2c329394-2">3‑LT can loosen and rapidly recur radiographic abnormalities; Mark‑Henry reconstructs both volar/dorsal but carries risks of fractures and lunate avascular necrosis</cite> <cite id="2c329394-3">Failure to suture the stronger palmar SL ligament and reliance on a palmar-only approach may increase complications</cite>.

Outcome measurement heterogeneity and rehabilitation windows
- Studies use different outcome instruments (DASH, QuickDASH, Mayo/Wrist scores, patient satisfaction) and radiographic/MRI healing criteria (RMLA thresholds, radiographic capno/SL gap, tunnel fill, SCAP index), which confound comparisons. Small series with patient‑reported gains may mask poor radiographic healing or persistent kinematic instability; conversely, radiographic “healing” without functional improvement can skew perceptions of success <cite id="94179f19-2">A series reported favorable DASH/Mayo and satisfaction after PL anchor reconstruction, but did not standardize radiographic healing assessment</cite> <cite id="2c329394-2">Reports of favorable results coexist with recurrent loosening and radiographic deterioration, underscoring inconsistent outcome definitions</cite>. 
- Rehabilitation protocols and return‑to‑activity timelines vary widely (e.g., time to remove K‑wires or start weight bearing), influencing ligamentization, scar quality, and symptom recovery. Case reports demonstrate bilateral SLL reconstruction with early protected mobilization and return to daily activities at 12 weeks, yet other cohorts emphasize prolonged immobilization before protected motion; these differences contribute to outcome variability and limit cross‑study synthesis <cite id="2c329394-4">A bilateral case used K‑wire plus bone anchor suture fixation, with antibiotics/analgesia, radiographic follow‑up, wire removal at 8 weeks, therapist sessions, and return to daily activities by 12 weeks</cite>. 
- Radiographic criteria differ (gap/tunnel fill vs MRI ligament continuity), and chronicity/osteonecrosis can mimic healing. Narrative reports emphasize revascularization benefits and less stiffness with palmar strategies, but without standardized imaging thresholds or follow‑up, favorable descriptions may reflect selection bias or incomplete assessment of cartilage and lunate viability <cite id="2c329394-3">Protection of blood supply and palmar-only approaches may reduce stiffness and necrosis in some cases, but complications still occur when palmar ligament is not adequately sutured</cite>.

Confounding by indication and patient/tendon factors
- Patient selection, comorbid carpal pathology, and surgeon experience differ across series, producing confounding. Reviews emphasize that surgical choice depends on severity, time since injury, and presence of degenerative change; acute, low‑cohort heterogeneity yields better outcomes, while chronic, high‑grade instability with arthritis or associated carpal injuries leads to mixed results regardless of technique <cite id="94179f19-4">Surgical indications depend on instability severity, time after trauma, and degenerative changes; acute repair is preferred for better results</cite> <cite id="2c329394-0">Indications vary with severity and timing; many techniques exist for chronic cases when immobilization fails</cite>. 
- Tendon/allograft availability and fixation modality shape technique adoption. Palmaris longus autografts and suture‑anchor fixation avoid tunnel drilling and may appeal to surgeons seeking low‑profile, pullout‑strong constructs; however, absence of standardized fixation protocols and incomplete palmar stabilization can lead to divergent complications and incomplete correction of multidirectional instability <cite id="94179f19-2">Palmaris longus suture‑anchor reconstruction provided satisfactory outcomes and avoids drilling through bone</cite> <cite id="2c329394-2">Complications with 3‑LT and Mark‑Henry suggest that technique-specific risks and incomplete multiplanar stabilization can drive poor outcomes</cite>.

Putting it together: mechanisms of conflict
- The same injury spectrum treated with different techniques yields distinct kinematic, biological, and healing profiles, so outcomes optimized for one construct (e.g., multidirectional tenodesis) may not transfer to another (e.g., palmar‑only anchor suspension) when patient/tendon biology or rehab loading differ <cite id="94179f19-3">Technique-dependent restoration of SL gap/angle across wrist positions shows why different reconstructions can lead to divergent stability outcomes</cite> <cite id="2c329394-2">Recurrent loosening, need for dual-volar-dorsal reconstruction, and associated complications explain poor or conflicting long-term results across methods</cite>. 
- Outcome heterogeneity (instruments and imaging criteria) and variable rehab windows can invert the relationship between mechanical and functional recovery across cohorts, making direct comparisons misleading unless standardized protocols and reporting thresholds are used <cite id="94179f19-2">Reported functional gains may not reflect standardized radiographic healing, and vice versa</cite> <cite id="2c329394-4">Early mobilization timelines vary, affecting ligamentization and symptom recovery</cite>. 
- Confounding by indication ensures that “better outcomes” in one series often reflect selection of less severe, more salvageable cases or more favorable biology/timing, while another series reports worse outcomes after attempting complex reconstructions in chronic arthritis—further widening apparent conflicts <cite id="94179f19-4">Technique selection is driven by severity, timing, and degenerative change; acute cases favor better outcomes, while chronic cases require reconstruction with variable success</cite>.

What evidence would narrow the gaps
- Head‑to‑head, prospectively powered trials comparing major technique families with standardized: 
  1) baseline MRI/CT quantification (SL gap, RMLA, lunate morphology), 
  2) identical rehabilitation algorithms with objective milestones, 
  3) harmonized outcome measures (DASH/QuickDASH, Mayo wrist score, patient global), 
  4) uniform healing definitions (e.g., RMLA thresholds, SCAP index, MRI continuity), and 
  5) minimum 2‑year follow‑up to capture recurrence/AVN and functional durability <cite id="2c329394-2">Because a single best method remains undetermined and complications vary by technique, standardized multi‑center trials are needed</cite>. 
- Biomechanics‑guided registry studies reporting gap/angle restoration, tunnel/bone stress, and patient‑reported outcomes by technique and patient subgroup (acute vs chronic; scaphoid varus‑derotation injury vs generalized SLIL; presence of arthritis) would clarify when each technique confers superior stability‑to‑function tradeoffs <cite id="94179f19-3">Technique-dependent gap/angle restoration across positions indicates subgroup-specific biomechanical effects</cite>.

Practical implications for centers reporting outcomes
- Align technique to biology and timing: prioritize early primary repair/capsulodesis for acute injury; for chronic instability with reducible scaphoid and minimal arthritis, consider multi‑junction tenodesis or bone‑ligament‑bone constructs; for complex rotatory subluxation/DISI, tailor tenodesis/capsulodesis to restore rotatory stability; and for high‑risk tunnel chondral injury, favor non‑tunnel suspensions with robust palmar/dorsal suture fixation <cite id="a8c1cae2-1">Chronicity dictates whether direct repair or reconstruction is possible; for rotatory subluxation and DISI, modified Brunelli and three‑ligament tenodesis are commonly used</cite> <cite id="2c329394-2">Bone‑ligament‑bone autografts and tenodesis are options in chronic cases without degenerative change; 3‑LT and Mark‑Henry each have characteristic risks</cite>. 
- Standardize fixation and rehab: ensure both volar and dorsal spans are tensioned and sutured (when using suspensions), document graft fixation mode (anchor vs bone tunnel/bridging), and adopt uniform protected motion and return‑to‑activity schedules to reduce variability in healing and complications <cite id="2c329394-2">Failure to address multidirectional instability can lead to rapid loosening; over‑constraint can cause lunate avascular necrosis</cite> <cite id="2c329394-3">Insufficient palmar ligament suture can produce limited ROM, necrosis, or sclerosis</cite>. 
- Report both radiographic and functional outcomes with explicit thresholds and follow‑up: include gap/angle metrics, healing criteria, and instrumented scores to contextualize stability‑function relationships and avoid misinterpretation of “healing” vs “symptom recovery” <cite id="94179f19-2">A series showed good function without standardized imaging-based healing criteria, underscoring the risk of divergent interpretations</cite>. 

Bottom line
Reported outcomes for SLL reconstruction conflict primarily because multiple materially distinct techniques impose different kinematic constraints, fixation mechanics, and biological demands on an increasingly heterogeneous patient cohort; outcomes are further confounded by injury timing/chronicity, variable graft/fixation choices, divergent rehabilitation protocols, and inconsistent outcome/healing definitions. Addressing these sources of heterogeneity—standardized indications, biomechanics‑guided technique selection, uniform fixation and rehab algorithms, and harmonized outcome/healing criteria—are essential to converge on technique‑specific expectations and resolve cross‑study conflicts <cite id="94179f19-4">Technique diversity and indication-based selection drive variable results; early management improves outcomes</cite> <cite id="94179f19-3">Different tenodesis methods restore stability variably across wrist positions</cite> <cite id="2c329394-2">No single best method exists; results are unsatisfactory in many cases and vary with technique-specific risks and patient factors</cite> <cite id="2c329394-3">Palmar-only or inadequate suture of the palmar SL ligament increases complication risk, creating conflicting outcome narratives</cite> <cite id="94179f19-2">Satisfactory functional scores can occur without standardized healing assessment, complicating cross-study comparisons</cite>.

- Even within tenodesis, subtypes differ biomechanically and clinically (e.g., Corella, SLAM, modified Brunelli), with cadaveric/FEA work showing technique‑dependent restoration of SL gap and angle across wrist positions; this mechanical variability plausibly maps to variable radiographic and patient‑reported outcomes across cohorts <cite id="94179f19-3">The Corella technique restored SL gap/angle closer to intact ligament than SLAM and modified Brunelli across flexion/extension/radial‑ulnar deviation, with multiple junction points between scaphoid and lunate being beneficial</cite>.

Biomechanical and fixation‑related reasons for conflicting outcomes
- Technique choice alters scapholunate kinematics and load sharing. Tenodesis methods that distribute load across multiple carpal ligaments may better resist multidirectional instability than single‑junction capsulodesis, but over‑constraint or malpositioning can cause complications (e.g., lunate necrosis, tunnel fractures) that worsen outcomes <cite id="2c329394-2">3‑LT has favorable but recurrent loosening and radiographic abnormalities; Mark‑Henry reconstructs both volar/dorsal limbs yet has complications including fractures and avascular necrosis of the lunate</cite> <cite id="94179f19-3">Corella outperformed SLAM and modified Brunelli in restoring gap/angle across wrist positions, supporting the value of multiple junction points</cite>. 
- Anchor‑based “suspension” strategies avoid drilling through bone for graft fixation and aim to harness high pullout strength, but outcomes depend on suture configuration, graft tensioning, and whether both palmar/dorsal spans are adequately fixed; small series suggest satisfactory results but broader experience shows variable radiographic healing and complications when compared across techniques <cite id="94179f19-2">Palmaris longus reconstruction with bone anchors achieved functional outcomes comparable to tenodesis and avoided drilling through bone</cite> <cite id="2c329394-1">A non–bone tunnel technique reported clinical outcomes, highlighting technique variation</cite>.

Biological/tissue and timing factors that shift outcomes
- Chronicity and scaphoid integrity fundamentally change tissue quality and healing potential. In acute injuries, early repair/capsulodesis yields better ligamentous healing; in chronic cases with degenerative change or irreparable SLIL, reconstructions (autograft, bone bridge) are often required, but outcomes degrade with advanced arthritis, cartilage injury, or persistent instability despite reconstruction <cite id="2c329394-0">Acute repair remains the gold standard because earlier intervention provides better results; for chronic injuries, ligament reconstruction is generally preferable, with many arthroscopic options when immobilization fails</cite> <cite id="2c329394-2">When degenerative change is present, best technique remains uncertain; bone‑ligament‑bone autografts and tenodesis are selected, yet results are unsatisfactory and a single best method is undetermined</cite>. 
- Graft choice and tissue quality modulate healing. Biomechanical loosening of tenodesis over time and the need to reconstruct both volar/dorsal limbs (as in Mark‑Henry) reflect biological creep and multidirectional insufficiency; complications like avascular necrosis may arise from altered load transfer and soft‑tissue handling, especially if palmar stabilizers are not robustly reconstructed <cite id="2c329394-2">3‑LT can loosen and rapidly recur radiographic abnormalities; Mark‑Henry reconstructs both volar/dorsal but carries risks of fractures and lunate avascular necrosis</cite> <cite id="2c329394-3">Failure to suture the stronger palmar SL ligament and reliance on a palmar-only approach may increase complications</cite>.

Outcome measurement heterogeneity and rehabilitation windows
- Studies use different outcome instruments (DASH, QuickDASH, Mayo/Wrist scores, patient satisfaction) and radiographic/MRI healing criteria (RMLA thresholds, radiographic capno/SL gap, tunnel fill, SCAP index), which confound comparisons. Small series with patient‑reported gains may mask poor radiographic healing or persistent kinematic instability; conversely, radiographic “healing” without functional improvement can skew perceptions of success <cite id="94179f19-2">A series reported favorable DASH/Mayo and satisfaction after PL anchor reconstruction, but did not standardize radiographic healing assessment</cite> <cite id="2c329394-2">Reports of favorable results coexist with recurrent loosening and radiographic deterioration, underscoring inconsistent outcome definitions</cite>. 
- Rehabilitation protocols and return‑to‑activity timelines vary widely (e.g., time to remove K‑wires or start weight bearing), influencing ligamentization, scar quality, and symptom recovery. Case reports demonstrate bilateral SLL reconstruction with early protected mobilization and return to daily activities at 12 weeks, yet other cohorts emphasize prolonged immobilization before protected motion; these differences contribute to outcome variability and limit cross‑study synthesis <cite id="2c329394-4">A bilateral case used K‑wire plus bone anchor suture fixation, with antibiotics/analgesia, radiographic follow‑up, wire removal at 8 weeks, therapist sessions, and return to daily activities by 12 weeks</cite>. 
- Radiographic criteria differ (gap/tunnel fill vs MRI ligament continuity), and chronicity/osteonecrosis can mimic healing. Narrative reports emphasize revascularization benefits and less stiffness with palmar strategies, but without standardized imaging thresholds or follow‑up, favorable descriptions may reflect selection bias or incomplete assessment of cartilage and lunate viability <cite id="2c329394-3">Protection of blood supply and palmar-only approaches may reduce stiffness and necrosis in some cases, but complications still occur when palmar ligament is not adequately sutured</cite>.

Confounding by indication and patient/tendon factors
- Patient selection, comorbid carpal pathology, and surgeon experience differ across series, producing confounding. Reviews emphasize that surgical choice depends on severity, time since injury, and presence of degenerative change; acute, low‑cohort heterogeneity yields better outcomes, while chronic, high‑grade instability with arthritis or associated carpal injuries leads to mixed results regardless of technique <cite id="94179f19-4">Surgical indications depend on instability severity, time after trauma, and degenerative changes; acute repair is preferred for better results</cite> <cite id="2c329394-0">Indications vary with severity and timing; many techniques exist for chronic cases when immobilization fails</cite>. 
- Tendon/allograft availability and fixation modality shape technique adoption. Palmaris longus autografts and suture‑anchor fixation avoid tunnel drilling and may appeal to surgeons seeking low‑profile, pullout‑strong constructs; however, absence of standardized fixation protocols and incomplete palmar stabilization can lead to divergent complications and incomplete correction of multidirectional instability <cite id="94179f19-2">Palmaris longus suture‑anchor reconstruction provided satisfactory outcomes and avoids drilling through bone</cite> <cite id="2c329394-2">Complications with 3‑LT and Mark‑Henry suggest that technique-specific risks and incomplete multiplanar stabilization can drive poor outcomes</cite>.

Putting it together: mechanisms of conflict
- The same injury spectrum treated with different techniques yields distinct kinematic, biological, and healing profiles, so outcomes optimized for one construct (e.g., multidirectional tenodesis) may not transfer to another (e.g., palmar‑only anchor suspension) when patient/tendon biology or rehab loading differ <cite id="94179f19-3">Technique-dependent restoration of SL gap/angle across wrist positions shows why different reconstructions can lead to divergent stability outcomes</cite> <cite id="2c329394-2">Recurrent loosening, need for dual-volar-dorsal reconstruction, and associated complications explain poor or conflicting long-term results across methods</cite>. 
- Outcome heterogeneity (instruments and imaging criteria) and variable rehab windows can invert the relationship between mechanical and functional recovery across cohorts, making direct comparisons misleading unless standardized protocols and reporting thresholds are used <cite id="94179f19-2">Reported functional gains may not reflect standardized radiographic healing, and vice versa</cite> <cite id="2c329394-4">Early mobilization timelines vary, affecting ligamentization and symptom recovery</cite>. 
- Confounding by indication ensures that “better outcomes” in one series often reflect selection of less severe, more salvageable cases or more favorable biology/timing, while another series reports worse outcomes after attempting complex reconstructions in chronic arthritis—further widening apparent conflicts <cite id="94179f19-4">Technique selection is driven by severity, timing, and degenerative change; acute cases favor better outcomes, while chronic cases require reconstruction with variable success</cite>.

What evidence would narrow the gaps
- Head‑to‑head, prospectively powered trials comparing major technique families with standardized: 
  1) baseline MRI/CT quantification (SL gap, RMLA, lunate morphology), 
  2) identical rehabilitation algorithms with objective milestones, 
  3) harmonized outcome measures (DASH/QuickDASH, Mayo wrist score, patient global), 
  4) uniform healing definitions (e.g., RMLA thresholds, SCAP index, MRI continuity), and 
  5) minimum 2‑year follow‑up to capture recurrence/AVN and functional durability <cite id="2c329394-2">Because a single best method remains undetermined and complications vary by technique, standardized multi‑center trials are needed</cite>. 
- Biomechanics‑guided registry studies reporting gap/angle restoration, tunnel/bone stress, and patient‑reported outcomes by technique and patient subgroup (acute vs chronic; scaphoid varus‑derotation injury vs generalized SLIL; presence of arthritis) would clarify when each technique confers superior stability‑to‑function tradeoffs <cite id="94179f19-3">Technique-dependent gap/angle restoration across positions indicates subgroup-specific biomechanical effects</cite>.

Practical implications for centers reporting outcomes
- Align technique to biology and timing: prioritize early primary repair/capsulodesis for acute injury; for chronic instability with reducible scaphoid and minimal arthritis, consider multi‑junction tenodesis or bone‑ligament‑bone constructs; for complex rotatory subluxation/DISI, tailor tenodesis/capsulodesis to restore rotatory stability; and for high‑risk tunnel chondral injury, favor non‑tunnel suspensions with robust palmar/dorsal suture fixation <cite id="a8c1cae2-1">Chronicity dictates whether direct repair or reconstruction is possible; for rotatory subluxation and DISI, modified Brunelli and three‑ligament tenodesis are commonly used</cite> <cite id="2c329394-2">Bone‑ligament‑bone autografts and tenodesis are options in chronic cases without degenerative change; 3‑LT and Mark‑Henry each have characteristic risks</cite>.

Bottom line
Reported outcomes for SLL reconstruction conflict primarily because multiple materially distinct techniques impose different kinematic constraints, fixation mechanics, and biological demands on an increasingly heterogeneous patient cohort; outcomes are further confounded by injury timing/chronicity, variable graft/fixation choices, divergent rehabilitation protocols, and inconsistent outcome/healing definitions. Snippet: There is currently no consensus on the best operative treatment for chronic scapholunate dissociation with an irreparable scapholunate interosseous ligament (SLIL) but without degenerative change [1]. Numerous reconstructive surgeries have been described in previous studies. Among them, dorsal capsulodesis, bone-ligament-bone autografts, scapholunate axis method (SLAM), reduction and association of the scaphoid and lunate (RASL), and a variety of tendon reconstruction methods are currently used [2][3][4][5][6][7][8]. However, the results of these procedures are unsatisfactory and the single most effective treatment for chronic scapholunate instability is yet to be determined [9]. 

The purpose of reconstruction is to address the scapholunate interval widening and scaphoid flexion deformity to prevent scapholunate advanced collapse arthritis in the future [10]. The most used reconstruction technique at present is three-ligament tenodesis (3LT) [8]. This technique incorporates some features from previously published reconstruction procedures using a strip of the flexor carpi radialis (FCR) tendon. It enhances the action of three ligaments (scaphotrapeziotrapezoid, dorsal scapholunate, dorsal radiotriquetral ligament) and has therefore been named the 3LT procedure [8]. Although 3LT is a reliable technique, with favorable results reported by several authors, ligamentous loosening did result in the rapid recurrence of radiological abnormalities and frequent complications [11][12][13]. 

To compensate for the ligamentous loosening of 3LT, the Mark-Henry technique (MHT) was introduced [14]. This technique reconstructs both the volar and dorsal limbs of the SLIL and addresses the multidirectional nature of scapholunate instability. However, the surgical procedure was somewhat complicated, and there were complications such as fractures and avascular necrosis of the lunate [15].

Title: Simultaneous palmar-divergent dislocation of scaphoid and lunate associated with ipsilateral humeroradial joint dislocation and humerus shaft fracture:a rare case report and proposal of an additional subtype
Snippet: Recently, the carpal interosseous ligament repair bene ts have been recognised in the preventment of late carpal instability, scapholunate dissociation, and avascular osteonecrosis. Short et al. have studied the ligamentous stabilisers of scaphoid and lunate and demonstrated that the scapholunate interosseous ligament is the primary stabiliser, and the others are secondary stabilisers of the scapholunate articulation (11). In our case, we only repaired the stronger palmar scapholunate ligament through single volar approach, even though scaphoid and lunate were not xed accurately, the patient had no avascular necrosis of carpal bones, which indicated that protection of blood supplies of scapholunate from surrounding soft tissue was effective for the scapholunate revascularisation. Reduction and ligament repair through only a palmar incision have greater advantages, as it is less invasive, easier operation, less damage to the blood supply and lower wrist stiffness. It has already reported that torn ligaments repair with a suture anchor make operation simplify and offer nonspace-consuming and permanent xation (7,9,12). Of previous reports, a total of 3 cases undertook xation of scapholunate or interosseous ligaments repaired by combined palmar and dorsal approaches, limited ROM to different extent occurred in all cases and avascular osteonecrosis or subchondral sclerosis of scapholunate in two cases and exion deformity of the scaphoid with a break in arc II of Gilula's line in one case, postoperatively (3,7,9). By analysis, we speculated that these complications might be closely related to additional dorsal incision and increasing damage to blood supplies or no suture of the stronger palmar scapholunate ligament. In this case, therefore, we renewed the surgical strategy to prevent those complications.

Title: Bilateral traumatic scapholunate dissociation: Case report
Snippet: The patient underwent bilateral scapholunate ligament reconstruction using bone anchor suture, and k wire fixation. The surgery was done by the senior author Dr. Almishal. Intraoperatively, the scapholunate ligament was found to be avulsed from the scaphoid bilaterally. Fixation was done using 2 size 0.45 k wires, fixing scaphoid to the lunate, and scaphoid to the capitate. The scapholunate ligaments were repaired using a bone anchor suture. After the surgery, he received oral antibiotic and analgesia for 1 week then he was followed up in outpatient clinic to assess the wounds and with regular X-rays. K-wires were removed after 8 weeks (Figs. 5-6). The patient has good active wrist and fingers flexion and extension. Also, he was referred to the hand therapist for active range of motion exercises and edema control. He received total of 6 sessions with the hand therapist. Patient returned to his daily life activities 12 weeks after the surgery.
